```{r libraries}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(stringr)
library(tidytext)
library(quanteda)
library(tibble)
```

```{r load_texts}
hw_dir <- "C:/Users/titin/OneDrive - Duke University/TAD/HW2/"

com_file   <- paste0(hw_dir, "A07594__Circle_of_Commerce.txt")
trade_file <- paste0(hw_dir, "B14801__Free_Trade.txt")
file_c     <- paste0(hw_dir, "A06785.txt")

com_txt   <- read_file(com_file)
trade_txt <- read_file(trade_file)
text_c    <- read_file(file_c)

texts <- tibble(
  doc_title = c("Commerce Text", "Trade Text", "Text C"),
  text = c(com_txt, trade_txt, text_c)
)

texts
```

```{r stopword_lists}
# Standard tidytext stopword list, as in Week 02
data("stop_words")
```


## Part I: Raw-Count Sentiment Analysis

### Step 1: Tokenize and clean the text

One cleaned set of tokens is created for all three documents. These same tokens are used for both the raw-count analysis (Part I) and the TF-IDF analysis (Part II).

```{r tokenize}
words_clean <- texts %>%
  unnest_tokens(word, text) %>%
  mutate(
    word = str_to_lower(word),
    word = str_replace_all(word, "ſ", "s")   # normalize the long s
  ) %>%
  anti_join(stop_words, by = "word")

words_clean
```

### 2: Join tokens to the Bing sentiment dictionary

```{r bing}
bing <- get_sentiments("bing")

# Only the Commerce and Trade texts are analyzed for sentiment
words_sentiment <- words_clean %>%
  filter(doc_title %in% c("Commerce Text", "Trade Text")) %>%
  inner_join(bing, by = "word")

words_sentiment
```

### 3: Compute raw sentiment totals

```{r sentiment}
raw_sentiment <- words_sentiment %>%
  count(doc_title, sentiment) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = sentiment,
    values_from = n,
    values_fill = 0
  ) %>%
  rename(raw_positive = positive, raw_negative = negative) %>%
  mutate(raw_net = raw_positive - raw_negative)

raw_sentiment
```


## Part II: TF-IDF-Weighted Sentiment Analysis

## Compute TF-IDF for words in each document

The DFM is built directly from the cleaned tidy tokens from Step 1 (`cast_dfm()`), so the text-cleaning decisions are identical across both analyses. All three documents are included so that IDF is calculated over the full corpus.

```{r tfidf}
corpus_dfm <- words_clean %>%
  count(doc_title, word) %>%
  cast_dfm(doc_title, word, n)

corpus_dfm

corpus_tfidf <- dfm_tfidf(corpus_dfm)
```

### Convert the TF-IDF results to a tidy table

```{r tfidf_tidy}
tfidf_tidy <- convert(corpus_tfidf, to = "data.frame") %>%
  rename(doc_title = doc_id) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -doc_title,
    names_to = "word",
    values_to = "tfidf"
  ) %>%
  filter(tfidf > 0) %>%
  # Text C was only needed to calculate IDF
  filter(doc_title %in% c("Commerce Text", "Trade Text"))

tfidf_tidy %>%
  arrange(desc(tfidf))
```

### Keep only sentiment-bearing words

```{r tfidf_sentiment}
tfidf_sentiment <- tfidf_tidy %>%
  inner_join(bing, by = "word")

top_tfidf_sentiment <- tfidf_sentiment %>%
  group_by(doc_title, sentiment) %>%
  slice_max(tfidf, n = 10, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  arrange(doc_title, sentiment, desc(tfidf))

print(top_tfidf_sentiment, n = Inf)
```

## Compute TF-IDF-weighted sentiment totals

```{r tfidf_totals}
tfidf_totals <- tfidf_sentiment %>%
  group_by(doc_title, sentiment) %>%
  summarise(weight = sum(tfidf), .groups = "drop") %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = sentiment,
    values_from = weight,
    values_fill = 0
  ) %>%
  rename(tfidf_positive = positive, tfidf_negative = negative) %>%
  mutate(tfidf_net = tfidf_positive - tfidf_negative)

tfidf_totals
```


##  Compare Raw vs. TF-IDF Sentiment

```{r comparison}
sentiment_comparison <- raw_sentiment %>%
  left_join(tfidf_totals, by = "doc_title") %>%
  select(doc_title,
         raw_positive, raw_negative, raw_net,
         tfidf_positive, tfidf_negative, tfidf_net)

print(sentiment_comparison, width = Inf)

write_csv(sentiment_comparison, paste0(hw_dir, "sentiment_comparison.csv"))
```

most frequent sentiment words under raw counts:

```{r top_words}
top_raw_words <- words_sentiment %>%
  count(doc_title, sentiment, word, sort = TRUE) %>%
  group_by(doc_title, sentiment) %>%
  slice_head(n = 10) %>%
  ungroup()

print(top_raw_words, n = Inf)
```


**What changed between the two methods?**

Under raw counts, both texts look positive. The Commerce Text has 491 positive and 423 negative words (+68), and the Trade Text has 344 positive and 281 negative words ( +63). After TF-IDF weighting, it flips for both texts and they become net negative. The Commerce Text had 63.0 positive and 86.3 negative (−23.3), and the Trade Text scores 32.7 positive and 44.2 negative (−11.5). Under raw counts the Texts' net scores are almost the same (68 vs. 63), even though the Commerce Text has many more sentiment words (914 vs. 625). Under TF-IDF, the Commerce Text's net score is about twice as negative as the Trade Text's.

**Why did TF-IDF alter the results?**

Raw counting gives every occurrence of a Bing word a weight of 1. TF-IDF multiplies each word's count by log10(3 / number of documents containing the word). A sentiment-containing word that appears in all three texts gets an IDF of 0 and no score, no matter how often it's used. Only words found in one or two texts keep any weight. Many of the most frequent sentiment words are shared across the three texts, because all three are about the same subject (trade, and exchange). Most of the raw positive count was made up of these shared words. Once they are removed, the remaining distinctive vocabulary leans negative. The TF-IDF score does not tell us that the texts are actually just negative, but rather that the sentiment words unique to each text are mostly negative

**Which specific words drove the changes?**

The most frequent negative words in the Commerce Text under raw counts were *decay* (14), *stranger* (13), *abuse* (12), *fall* (11), *false* (10), and *mystery* (9), one of which appear among the highest TF-IDF words. If they were in only one or two texts, their TF-IDF weight would be large enough to reach the top-10 list, so they must appear in all three document. TF-IDF results more impacted by words that appear only in one text. In the Commerce Text these are negative words;*impertinent* (2.86), *imperfect* (2.39) and positive words like *passion* (4.29), *divine* (3.34), and *affection* (2.86). In the Trade Text, all five of the highest-weighted sentiment words are negative: *imposition* (3.34), *disorderly* (2.86), *deficient*, *pleas*, and *loose*. It's highest-weighted words indicate Free Trade's complaints about taxes and charges on trade not just a generally negative mood.

**When would each method be more appropriate? What limitation does document length create for the raw-count measure?**

From the change with the TF-IDF scores, we can see that raw counts are more appropriate for describing a text's overall tone when documents are similar in length. TF-IDF is more appropriate for finding what makes a text's language distinctive within the corpus, though with only three documents its results should be cautiously interpreted. Document length is the main limitation of raw counts. The Commerce Text is significantly longer than the Trade Text (~ 34,000 vs. 20,000 tokens), so it has more positive and negative words simply because it has more words. Its raw net (+68) looks higher than the Trade Text's (+63), but as a share of sentiment words the Trade Text is more positive (10% vs. 7%). Raw scores should be normalized before comparing texts of different lengths.

## Challenge Extension: Sentiment Concentration vs. Diffusion

```{r ext}
total_weight <- tfidf_sentiment %>%
  group_by(doc_title) %>%
  summarise(total_sentiment_weight = sum(tfidf))

top5 <- tfidf_sentiment %>%
  group_by(doc_title) %>%
  slice_max(tfidf, n = 5, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  ungroup()

top5

top5 %>%
  group_by(doc_title) %>%
  summarise(top5_weight = sum(tfidf)) %>%
  left_join(total_weight, by = "doc_title") %>%
  mutate(top5_share = round(top5_weight / total_sentiment_weight, 3))
```

In both texts, sentiment is spread across many words rather than concentrated in a few. The top five words carry only 10.5% of the sentiment weight in the Commerce Text and 13.6% in the Trade Text. The Trade Text is slightly more concentrated, and all five of its top words are negative.
